title: Clouds and Weather Forecasts
summary: How clouds form from water vapor, what different cloud types tell us, how rain falls, and how meteorologists use data to forecast the weather.
poll: Weather forecasts are worth checking every day.

versions.title: Clouds in the Sky
versions.text:
Look up. Do you see a cloud? A cloud is made of tiny drops. We call them droplets.

The sun warms the sea. Some of it turns to a gas. The gas is water vapor. You can not see it. It goes up.

High up, the air is cold. The vapor turns back to drops. Each drop forms on a speck of dust. The drops float. Lots of drops make a cloud.

Some clouds are big and puffy. Some are flat and gray. Some are thin, like white hair.

In a cloud, the drops bump. They join and grow. Then they are too big to float. They fall as rain.

A storm can bring rain, wind, and dust. When will it come? A forecast tells us. It tells us what the sky will do.

Tools on the ground check the air. A satellite in space snaps shots of clouds. A computer helps us guess. The next few days are not hard to guess. Far days are hard.

In Saudi Arabia, rain is rare. But a big storm can fill a dry valley fast. A forecast helps keep us safe.

versions.title: Clouds in the Sky
versions.text:
Look up at the sky. Do you see a cloud? A cloud is made of water. It is made of tiny drops called droplets.

The sun warms the sea and the land. Some of the water turns into a gas. This gas is water vapor. You can not see it. It rises up into the air.

High in the sky, the air is cold. The cold makes the vapor turn back into drops. Each drop forms on a speck of dust or salt. The drops are so small that they float. Lots of them make a cloud.

Some clouds are big and puffy. Some are flat and gray. Some are thin, like white hair.

In a cloud, the droplets bump. They join and grow. When they get too heavy to float, they fall as rain.

A storm can bring rain, strong wind, and dust. When will a storm come? A forecast tells us. It tells what the weather will be like.

Tools on the ground check the air. A satellite in space takes photos of the clouds. A computer helps people guess what comes next. The next few days are not hard to guess. Days far off are hard.

In Saudi Arabia, it does not rain much. But a big storm can fill a dry valley fast. A good forecast helps keep people safe.

versions.title: What Clouds Can Tell Us
versions.text:
Look up on a cloudy day. The clouds may look like cotton, but they are made of water. Each cloud holds millions of tiny drops called droplets.

Where does the water come from? The sun heats seas, lakes, and wet ground. Some of the water turns into a gas called water vapor. You can not see it, but it is all around you. Warm air carries it up into the sky.

High above the ground, the air is much colder. The cold turns the vapor back into tiny drops. Each drop forms on a speck of dust, salt, or smoke. The drops are so light that they float. Lots of them make a cloud.

Clouds come in different shapes. Some are big and puffy. Some are flat gray sheets. Some are thin and wispy, high up in the sky.

Inside a cloud, droplets bump and join. They grow bigger and heavier. When they are too heavy to float, they fall as rain.

A storm can bring heavy rain, strong winds, or dust. That is why people make a weather forecast. It tells what the weather will most likely be.

Weather experts use tools on the ground to check the air. A satellite in space takes pictures of the clouds. Computers help put all the facts together. Forecasts for the next few days are quite good. Forecasts far ahead are harder.

In Saudi Arabia, rain is rare. But a sudden storm can flood a dry valley fast. A forecast can warn people to stay safe.

versions.title: What Clouds Can Tell Us
versions.text:
On a cloudy day, the sky can look like it is full of cotton. But clouds are not soft or dry. They are made of millions of tiny water droplets, or bits of ice, that float in the air.

The water in clouds comes from the ground. The sun heats oceans, lakes, rivers, and wet soil. Some of that water turns into a gas called water vapor. You can not see it. Warm air carries the vapor up into the sky.

As the air rises, it cools down. Cold air can not hold as much vapor, so the vapor turns back into tiny drops. Each drop forms on a speck of dust, sea salt, or smoke. The drops are so light that they float. When billions of them gather, we see a cloud.

Clouds come in many shapes. Puffy white clouds most often mean fair weather, but they can grow into tall storm clouds. Flat gray clouds can cover the whole sky and bring light rain. Thin, wispy clouds float very high and are made of ice.

Inside a cloud, droplets bump into each other and join. When they get too heavy to float, they fall as rain.

A storm can bring heavy rain, strong winds, or blowing dust. To get ready, people need a weather forecast. It tells what the weather will most likely be like in the next days.

Weather experts get facts about the air from tools on the ground. A satellite in space sends pictures of the clouds. Then strong computers use all of this to make a forecast. Forecasts for the next few days are most often right, but forecasts far ahead are less sure.

In Saudi Arabia, rain does not fall often. But a sudden storm can flood a dry valley in minutes. Forecasts help warn people so they can stay safe.

versions.title: Clouds and Weather Forecasts
versions.text:
On a cloudy afternoon, the sky can look like it is stuffed with cotton. Yet clouds are not soft or dry at all. Each one is made of millions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. They float together in the air.

The water in a cloud begins on the ground. The sun warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp soil. Some of that water begins to evaporate. It turns into an invisible gas called water vapor. Warm air rises. It carries the vapor high into the sky.

As the air rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much vapor, so the vapor begins to condense, or change back into liquid. Each droplet forms around a speck of dust, sea salt, or smoke. Billions of these droplets together make a cloud we can see.

Scientists sort clouds by their shapes. Cumulus clouds are puffy and white. They usually mean fair weather. On hot days, though, they can grow into tall thunderstorm clouds. Stratus clouds are flat gray sheets that can bring drizzle. Cirrus clouds are thin and wispy. They float very high, where it is so cold that they are made of ice.

Inside a cloud, droplets bump into one another and join together. When they become too heavy to stay up, they fall as rain.

A meteorologist is a scientist who studies the weather. Meteorologists collect facts from weather stations on the ground. They also use balloons that rise into the sky. Satellites in space send pictures of clouds. Then computers use all of this to predict what will happen next. Forecasts for the next few days are usually correct, but predictions for weeks ahead are much less certain.

In Saudi Arabia, rain is rare, but a sudden storm can flood a dry valley within minutes. Forecasts and warnings help people stay safe.

versions.title: Clouds, Data, and the Science of Forecasting
versions.text:
On a cloudy afternoon, the sky may appear to be stuffed with cotton, yet clouds are neither soft nor dry. Each one consists of millions of microscopic water droplets or ice crystals, suspended together in the atmosphere and drifting wherever the wind carries them.

The water in a cloud begins its journey at the surface of the planet. Sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp soil, causing some of the water to evaporate and become water vapor, an invisible gas. The amount of vapor in the air is called humidity. Because warm air is less dense than the cooler air surrounding it, it rises and transports the vapor high above the ground.

As the air ascends, it gradually cools, and because cooler air cannot hold as much vapor as warmer air, the vapor begins to change back into liquid. This process is called condensation. Each droplet forms around a microscopic particle of dust, sea salt, or smoke, and when billions of droplets accumulate in one place, a visible cloud appears.

Scientists classify clouds according to their shapes and altitudes. Cumulus clouds are puffy and white, and they usually indicate pleasant conditions, although on hot afternoons they can develop into towering thunderstorm clouds. Stratus clouds form flat gray layers that frequently produce drizzle. Cirrus clouds are delicate and feathery, floating at such great heights that they are composed entirely of ice.

Inside a cloud, droplets continually collide and combine, and when they become too heavy for the rising air to support, they fall as precipitation.

Meteorologists, the scientists who study the atmosphere, gather measurements of temperature, humidity, wind, and air pressure from ground stations and from balloons that carry instruments into the sky. Satellites photograph clouds from orbit, while radar detects falling rain. Powerful computers combine this data to predict future conditions. The accuracy of forecasts for the next few days is generally high, although predictions for several weeks ahead remain considerably less reliable.

In Saudi Arabia, rainfall is relatively uncommon, but a sudden storm can flood a dry valley within minutes, so accurate forecasts and official warnings help communities prepare.

versions.title: Clouds, Data, and the Science of Forecasting
versions.text:
On an overcast afternoon, the sky may appear to be stuffed with cotton, yet clouds are neither soft nor dry, since each one consists of millions of microscopic water droplets or ice crystals suspended together in the atmosphere and drifting wherever the prevailing winds transport them.

The water in a cloud originates at the surface of the planet. Solar energy warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp soil, causing some of the water to evaporate and become water vapor, an invisible gas whose concentration in the air is described as humidity. Because warm air is less dense than the cooler air surrounding it, it rises buoyantly and transports the vapor high above the ground. It may climb for several kilometers before it stops.

As the air ascends, it progressively cools, and because cooler air cannot retain as much vapor as warmer air, the vapor begins to revert to liquid through a process known as condensation. Each droplet forms around a microscopic particle of dust, sea salt, or smoke, and when billions of droplets accumulate in a particular location, a visible cloud materializes.

Scientists classify clouds according to their characteristic formations and altitudes. Cumulus clouds are puffy and white, and they typically indicate pleasant conditions, although on sweltering afternoons they can develop into towering thunderstorm clouds. Stratus clouds form flat gray layers that frequently produce drizzle, whereas cirrus clouds are delicate and feathery, floating at such tremendous altitudes that they are composed entirely of ice.

Inside a cloud, droplets continually collide and combine, and when they become too heavy for the rising air to support, they descend as precipitation. This precipitation may reach the ground as rain, as hail, or, in colder places, as snow.

Meteorologists, the scientists who investigate atmospheric behavior, gather continuous measurements of temperature, humidity, wind velocity, and air pressure from ground stations and from balloons that carry instruments into the stratosphere. Satellites photograph clouds from orbit, while radar identifies precipitation, and sophisticated computers integrate this information to predict future conditions. The accuracy of forecasts for the immediate future is generally impressive, although predictions for several weeks ahead remain considerably less dependable. Small changes that no one measured can slowly grow into large differences.

In Saudi Arabia, rainfall is relatively infrequent, but a sudden storm can inundate a dry valley within minutes, so accurate forecasts and official warnings help communities prepare and avoid danger.

questions.stem: In the article, water vapor is described as a gas you can not see. What does vapor mean?

Water that has turned into a gas

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Cirrus clouds are the most important clouds for forecasting.
Clouds form through evaporation and condensation, and meteorologists combine many measurements to forecast weather.
Computers have replaced meteorologists in forecasting the weather.
Saudi Arabia receives more rain than most countries.
questions.why: The article traces the water cycle that creates clouds and rain and then explains how scientists gather and combine data to predict weather.

wrong.A: Cirrus clouds are one type described; the article does not rank them as most important.
wrong.C: The article says meteorologists gather data and computers integrate it; people are not replaced.
wrong.D: The article says rainfall in Saudi Arabia is relatively infrequent.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is humidity?
options: The temperature of the air near the ground on a hot day
The speed of the wind
The concentration of water vapor in the air
The height of a cloud
questions.why: The article defines humidity as the quantity or concentration of water vapor in the air.

wrong.A: Temperature is measured separately from humidity.
wrong.B: Wind is listed as a different measurement.
wrong.D: Cloud height is altitude, not humidity.

questions.stem: Which tool does the article say detects falling rain?
options: Weather balloons
Ground thermometers
Satellites
Radar
questions.why: The article states that radar detects or identifies falling rain (precipitation).

wrong.A: Balloons carry instruments that measure the air higher up.
wrong.B: Ground stations measure temperature and other conditions.

questions.stem: The article says a visible cloud 'materializes' when billions of droplets accumulate. What does materializes mean?
options: Appears or comes into view
Breaks apart into many smaller pieces and disappears
Turns into a solid
Moves toward the ground
questions.why: Before the droplets gather, nothing is visible; when they accumulate, the cloud becomes visible, so materializes means appears.

wrong.B: The droplets are coming together, not breaking apart.
wrong.C: Most cloud droplets stay liquid; the word is about becoming visible.
wrong.D: The sentence is about the cloud appearing, not falling.

questions.stem: Why does water vapor condense as air rises?
options: Rising air gets warmer and pushes water out.
Rising air cools, and cooler air cannot retain as much vapor.
Dust particles absorb heat from the sun and then quickly freeze the vapor.
Radar waves turn the vapor into liquid.
questions.why: The article explains that ascending air cools, and because cooler air cannot hold as much vapor as warmer air, the vapor turns into liquid.

wrong.A: Rising air cools; it does not get warmer.
wrong.C: Particles give droplets a surface to form on; the article does not say they freeze vapor.
wrong.D: Radar only detects rain; it does not change vapor.

questions.stem: A forecaster sees that humidity is high and cumulus clouds are growing taller on a hot afternoon. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Clear, calm weather is certain.
A thunderstorm may develop.
Cirrus clouds will soon replace them.
The air pressure is not worth measuring.
questions.why: The article says cumulus clouds can develop into towering thunderstorm clouds on hot afternoons, and high humidity means plenty of water for clouds.

wrong.A: Growing clouds and high humidity suggest a storm, not certain calm weather.
wrong.C: Nothing in the article says cumulus clouds turn into cirrus.
wrong.D: The article lists air pressure as an important measurement.

questions.stem: Why does the article mention that forecasts for several weeks ahead are less dependable?
options: To show that forecasting has limits even with modern technology
To argue that meteorologists should stop forecasting
To prove that satellites are broken
To suggest that only Saudi forecasts are reliable
questions.why: Even after describing satellites, radar, and computers, the author notes that long-range forecasts remain less dependable, showing the limits of prediction.

wrong.B: The article praises the accuracy of short-range forecasts and does not say to stop.
wrong.D: The article does not compare the reliability of different countries' forecasts.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with the example of Saudi Arabia?
options: To show that clouds never form over deserts
To connect the science to a real danger that forecasts help people prepare for
To explain how cirrus clouds are made of ice
To describe the history of weather satellites
questions.why: The final paragraph explains that sudden storms can flood dry valleys, showing why accurate forecasts and warnings matter to communities.

wrong.A: The paragraph says storms do happen in Saudi Arabia.
wrong.C: Cirrus clouds are explained in an earlier paragraph.
wrong.D: The article does not tell the history of satellites.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say weather forecasts are not worth checking because they are sometimes wrong. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that forecasts are not worth checking just because they are sometimes wrong. The article explains that meteorologists combine data from weather stations, balloons, satellites, and powerful computers, which is why forecasts for the next few days are usually accurate even though predictions weeks ahead are far less certain. This accuracy matters enormously in Saudi Arabia, where rain is uncommon but a sudden storm can flood a dry valley within minutes, so a forecast's warning can genuinely keep a family safe.
